title: True faith name-fight: Reformed reserve true for saving; Rome allows both senses
source_text: XLV. An autem fides illa mortua atque otiosa vera fides dici debeat, inter se disputant Scholae utriusque Doctores. Veram esse communiter affirmant Scholae Romanae Theologi, Reformati vero negant. Sed videtur esse merum de nomine certamen. Nam Doctores Reformati verae fidei titulum tribuendum putant illi soli fidei quae revera homines salvat & justificat, quo sensu fidem mortuam veram esse non docent Scholae Romanae Doctores: imo eorum nonnulli patiuntur eo respectu, ut vidimus, verae fidei nomen ad fidem vivam restringi. Sed tamen fidei etiam mortuae atque otiosae verae fidei titulum jure tribui posse volunt, quoniam est assensus, qui non omnino ficte, sed vere Dei verbo adhibetur, quique reapse fides in Scriptura vocatur, & revera est donum Spiritus Sancti, & perfectio quaedam mentis humanae, qua in boni salutaris notitia illustratur, quod Theologi Reformati non negant.
pass_a_gloss: But whether that dead and idle faith ought to be called true faith, the Doctors of both schools dispute among themselves. The theologians of the Roman school commonly affirm it is true; the Reformed deny it. But it seems a mere contest about a name. For the Reformed Doctors think the title of true faith should be given only to that faith which truly saves and justifies people — in which sense the Roman Doctors do not teach dead faith to be true; indeed some of them allow, as we have seen, the name of true faith to be restricted to living faith. Yet they still want the title of true faith to be rightly given even to dead and idle faith, because it is an assent applied not entirely fictitiously but truly to God word, and which is in fact called faith in Scripture, and truly is a gift of the Holy Spirit and a certain perfection of the human mind by which it is illuminated in the knowledge of saving good — which the Reformed theologians do not deny.
pass_b_english: Whether dead idle faith is true faith is largely a name fight: Reformed reserve true for saving faith; Rome often allows true also for real Spirit-gifted assent.
Even Romans who restrict true to living faith still call dead faith true as non-feigned assent, Scriptural faith, and a Spirit gift lighting saving good — which Reformed do not deny.
